summary: Describes the Server Cache Synchronization Protocol, which keeps the caches of related servers in agreement. It is written mainly for non-broadcast multi-access networks, though it can be adapted for broadcast ones.

plainLanguage.summary: Several helpers each keep a notebook. This describes how they trade notes so all of them have the same information.

subtitle: How a group of redundant servers keeps their caches identical by flooding changes to each other, much like a link-state routing protocol.

tldr.problem: A single server is a single point of failure, but with several servers each one must learn quickly about every change another one sees, without heavy load and without clients having to know every server.
tldr.mechanism: SCSP borrows its approach from OSPF: neighbors confirm they can hear each other (Hello), compare summaries of their caches (Cache Alignment), then reliably flood each new change to every neighbor except the one it came from (Cache State Update).
tldr.outcome: On its own SCSP is not useful: it must be paired with a protocol specific document, such as RFC 2335 for NHRP, that says what goes into the cache entries.

facts.label: Message type codes
facts.value: CA 1, CSU Request 2, CSU Reply 3, CSUS 4, Hello 5

today: RFC 2334 is a Proposed Standard from April 1998 and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC points to RFC 2335 as the NHRP specific companion.

sections.title: The Problem SCSP Solves
sections.content:
Relying on one server in a client/server design leaves a single point of failure. Even with redundant servers there is still the cache synchronization problem: when one server notices a change of state, it must pass that knowledge to every server that mirrors the same information, in a timely way and without putting undue strain on the servers.

The Server Cache Synchronization Protocol (SCSP) synchronizes the caches, or a portion of them, of a set of servers that are bound together in a Server Group (SG). The RFC is written for Non Broadcast Multiple Access (NBMA) networks, though usage on broadcast networks is described as fairly straightforward. Its stated design goals include scalability, use of auto-configuration, support for a range of authentication methods, and no need for clients to know about all the servers.

SCSP is not a stand-alone protocol. It must be coupled with an SCSP protocol specific specification that defines how a given client/server protocol uses it. The RFC names RFC 2335 (a distributed NHRP service) as one such document.
sections.plainLanguage: If only one helper keeps the notebook and they get sick, nobody knows anything. So you keep several copies, and you need a way for everyone to update their copy quickly when something changes.

sections.title: Server Groups and Roles
sections.content:
A Server Group is just a set of servers gathered around some commonality, for example all the NHRP servers belonging to a Logical IP Subnet. The client/server protocol being synchronized is named by a Protocol ID (PID), and the specific instance by a Server Group ID (SGID), a 16 bit value. The PID/SGID pair identifies one running instance of SCSP, so several instances can be synchronized independently.

All statements are made from the point of view of one server, the Local Server (LS). A Directly Connected Server (DCS) is one hop away, for example over a virtual circuit. A Remote Server (RS) is two or more hops away. Apart from this frame of reference, the RFC says there is no difference in functionality between an LS, a DCS and an RS.

SCSP places no topological requirement on the group, but the resulting graph must span all the servers to be synchronized. It borrows its distribution mechanism from link state protocols, but there is no mandatory Shortest Path First calculation and no memory beyond what the cache needs anyway.
sections.plainLanguage: Each helper looks at the world from where they stand. The neighbors they can talk to directly are one step away, and everyone else is farther off. Groups can have many separate notebooks, each tracked on its own.

sections.title: The Hello Protocol
sections.content:
SCSP has three sub protocols: Hello, Cache Alignment and Cache State Update. The Hello protocol finds out whether a DCS is operational and whether the connection to it is bidirectional, unidirectional or non-functional. Every LS MUST periodically send Hello messages to its DCSs. The LS is configured with the NBMA addresses of its would-be DCSs; how that configuration happens is outside the document.

For each DCS the LS runs a Hello Finite State Machine (HFSM). It starts in Down and moves to Waiting once NBMA level connectivity exists, then starts sending Hellos. Each Hello carries the sender's ID, a list of Receiver IDs (the DCSs recently heard from), a HelloInterval and a DeadFactor. If a received Hello lists the LS's own ID, the state becomes Bidirectional Connection; otherwise it becomes Unidirectional Connection.

If no Hello naming the LS arrives within HelloInterval * DeadFactor seconds, the DCS is considered stalled. The state then falls to Unidirectional if any Hellos were heard in that time, or to Waiting if none were. A malformed message or other abnormal event sends the machine to Waiting, and loss of NBMA connectivity sends it to Down. Until the state is Bidirectional, all non-Hello SCSP messages MUST be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: Neighbors keep saying hello and listing who they have heard. Once each side hears its own name in the other's hello, they know the line works both ways and can start trading notes.

sections.title: Cache Alignment
sections.content:
When the Hello state reaches Bidirectional, the Cache Alignment Finite State Machine (CAFSM) for that DCS leaves Down and enters Master/Slave Negotiation. The states that follow are Cache Summarize, Update Cache and Aligned. If the Hello state ever leaves Bidirectional, the CAFSM drops back to Down.

The first Cache Alignment (CA) message an LS sends has no records and has the M, I and O bits set. The server with the larger ID becomes master and sets the tempo; the other becomes slave. The two then take turns, in lock step, sending CA messages that carry summary records (CSAS records) of their cache entries, and the slave copies the master's CA sequence number. Retransmission is driven by the CAReXmtInterval timer.

While processing a CA message, the LS builds a CSA Request List of entries that are more up to date at the DCS. In the Update Cache state it sends CSU Solicit (CSUS) messages for those entries and the DCS answers with full records. With the CSUSReXmtInterval timer it re-asks for anything missing. When the cache is fully updated the state becomes Aligned.
sections.plainLanguage: When two helpers meet, they first pick who leads. Then they read each other short lists of what they know, ask for the details of anything newer, and when both lists match they are in sync.

sections.title: Cache State Updates and Newness
sections.content:
Once aligned, servers use Cache State Update (CSU) messages. A CSU Request carries one or more Cache State Advertisement (CSA) records, each a snapshot of one cache entry. An LS sends one when it sees a change, such as a client adding or removing an entry, or an entry timing out, being refreshed or being administratively modified. If the change came from a DCS, the LS forwards it to all its other DCSs. If it originated locally, it sends it to all of them. That is how a change floods through the group.

Receivers acknowledge with a CSU Reply that lists the summary (CSAS) records of the CSAs they accepted. A sender keeps unacknowledged CSAs on a per-DCS retransmit queue with a CSUReXmtInterval timer, holding only the newest version of an entry. After a configured number of failed retransmissions, an abnormal event occurs and the Hello state returns to Waiting.

A record is more up to date than a cache entry when the Cache Key and the Originator ID match and its CSA Sequence Number is greater. If a CSUS asks for an entry that has since vanished, the LS replies with a Null record by setting the N bit.

For point to multipoint connections, a root MAY send a CSU Request to the Receiver ID of all 0xFF bytes; receivers MUST then unicast their CSU Reply back to the sender.
sections.plainLanguage: When a helper learns something new, they tell every neighbor except the one who told them. Neighbors say thanks, and if no thanks comes back, the message is sent again. Whoever has the bigger version number wins.

sections.title: Message Formats
sections.content:
SCSP packets are carried with LLC/SNAP encapsulation: LLC 0xAA-AA-03, OUI 0x00-00-5e and PID 0x00-05. Every packet has three parts: a fixed part, a mandatory part and an optional extensions part. The fixed part holds the version (currently 1), a type code, the packet size, a standard IP checksum and a Start Of Extensions offset (zero if there are none).

The type codes are CA (1), CSU Request (2), CSU Reply (3), CSUS (4) and Hello (5). The mandatory part starts with a common block: Protocol ID, Server Group ID, flags, sender and receiver ID lengths, a record count and the variable length IDs. Protocol IDs defined so far are ATMARP (1), NHRP (2), MARS (3), DHCP (4) and LNNI (5).

A CSAS record holds a hop count, record length, key lengths, the N bit, a signed 32 bit CSA Sequence Number, the Cache Key and the Originator ID. A CSA record is a CSAS record followed by protocol specific data. The sequence number value 0x80000000 is reserved, the first one used is 0x80000001, and an entry nearing 0x7fffffff must first be purged from the group before it restarts at the bottom.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message starts with a little label saying what kind it is and how long it is, then who it is from and for, and then the actual notes.

sections.title: Authentication and Security
sections.content:
Extensions are type/length/value triplets ended by an End of Extensions entry. Two are defined: the Authentication Extension (type 1) and a Vendor-Private Extension (type 2). Whether to use authentication is a local matter. It works pairwise between an LS and a DCS and carries a Security Parameter Index and a message authentication code over the whole SCSP payload. The default algorithm is HMAC-MD5-128, and manual keying MUST be supported. A packet that fails the check is discarded and logged.

The RFC is frank about the limits. SCSP has a peer to peer trust model, and integrity covers the whole message rather than each record. Any properly authenticated server is trusted and its data is spread through the group, so one compromised server can corrupt the whole database. Without authentication, servers are open to spoofing, active and passive attacks. There is no encryption; a layer 3 mechanism is assumed. Every server can still be hit by denial of service, though authentication stops bogus packets from corrupting databases.
sections.plainLanguage: Neighbors can sign their messages with a secret code so fakes get thrown away. But if one trusted neighbor goes bad, they can fool everybody, so everyone should use the same safety rules.

messages.label: CSU Request
messages.note: Carries a CSA record describing a changed cache entry.

messages.label: CSU Reply
messages.note: Carries the CSAS record to acknowledge it.

messages.label: CSUS
messages.note: Solicits the full record for an entry the DCS holds in a newer form.

messages.label: CSU Request
messages.note: Answers with the whole cached information.

fields.name: Version
fields.desc: Version of SCSP; the current version is 1.

fields.name: Type Code
fields.desc: Message type: CA, CSU Request, CSU Reply, CSUS or Hello.

fields.name: Packet Size
fields.desc: Total length of the SCSP packet in octets.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: Standard IP checksum over the entire SCSP packet.

fields.name: Start Of Extensions
fields.desc: Zero if there are no extensions, otherwise the offset of the first extension.

items.label: CA
items.desc: Cache Alignment: summaries used to synchronize whole caches.

items.label: CSU Request
items.desc: Carries CSA records that report changed cache entries.

items.label: CSU Reply
items.desc: Acknowledges CSA records with CSAS records.

items.label: CSUS
items.desc: Cache State Update Solicit: asks for full CSA records.

items.label: Hello
items.desc: Checks connectivity with a directly connected server.
